title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Deconstructing Today's Price: The Scarcity Premium in Numbers

web_blocks.html: At the November 20, 2026 session close of $1,102.15 ($1,094.01 on the November 23 TradingView snapshot and $1,093.28 on Finviz), Costco carries a $488.40 billion market cap ($484.79 billion on November 23) [26, 27]. On November 10, 2026, the board declared a $30.00 per share special cash dividend (~$13.3 billion payable December 4, 2026) [19, 32]. That payout trims pre-dividend net cash from ~$15.1 billion ex-leases ($21,301 million cash against $6,162 million debt, including $2,248 million current maturities) to ~$1.8 billion ex-leases, and reduces FY2027 interest income from FY2026's $711 million level [1, 19, 32]. On audited FY2026 earnings of $20.76 per diluted share and $9,382 million of free cash flow ($15,817 million CFO less $6,435 million capex), shares trade at 53.09x trailing P/E (52.66x Finviz Nov 23), 43.50x forward P/E, 32.96x EV/EBITDA, and 52.06x Price-to-FCF (51.64x Finviz Nov 23, a 1.92% trailing FCF yield) [1, 26, 27].

Why does a physical retailer with an 11.09% merchandise gross margin and 3.85% operating margin trade at software multiples [1, 27]? The market is pricing in three traits at once. First, earnings are steady: $5,907 million in fees form an annuity floor equal to 50.6% of operating income [1, 18]. Second, negative working capital and 21.23% ROIC let Costco self-fund 28 net annual store openings while returning $13.3 billion in cash [1, 19, 27]. Third, defensive funds have crowded into the stock during a choppy macro tape [27, 28, 29]. That crowding pushed trailing P/E 48% above its 10-year mean of 35.86x and Price-to-Book (13.54x–13.65x) 44%–45% above its 9.40x mean [27, 28, 29].

web_blocks.takeaway: Every major multiple sits 34% to 55% above Costco's 10-year average [27, 28, 29]. That premium leaves zero margin of safety if multiples compress [27, 28, 29].

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Reverse DCF: What Growth Rate Is Already Baked Into $1,102.15?

web_blocks.html: Instead of guessing a single target, a Reverse DCF solves for the growth baked into today's $488.40 billion market cap [26, 27]. We use an 8.5% cost of equity and a 3.5% terminal growth rate [26, 27]. Starting from audited FY2026 FCF of $9,382 million ($15,817 million CFO less $6,435 million capex), we also note FY2027 capex rises 16.5% to ~$7.5 billion [1, 16, 30]. To earn an 8.5% annual return, Costco must grow FCF at 14.0% to 14.5% per year for ten straight years [1, 16, 30]. That requires ~$35 billion in annual FCF by FY2036 [1, 16, 30].

Now compare that hurdle against Costco's audited 10-year track record from Pass 1 [1, 7]. From FY2017 to FY2026, revenue grew at 9.96% per year and operating income at 12.31% [1, 7]. Net income grew 14.72% per year, helped by 2017 U.S. tax cuts and interest income on cash [1, 7]. Consensus 5-year forward EPS growth sits at just 9.81% [27]. Meanwhile, accrued member rewards rose 13.4% YoY to $3,037 million, ~$500 million of IEEPA tariff claims remain in flux alongside three consumer class actions, and ~$13.3 billion in cash leaves the balance sheet on December 4 [1, 31, 32]. If sales grow 7.5%–8.5% over the next decade and operating margin edges from 3.85% to 4.10%, FCF compounds closer to 9%–10%, pointing to fair value near $850–$950 per share [30].

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF & Multiple-Normalization Intrinsic Value Check
web_blocks.the_number: $990.00 base-case 12–18 month fair value (vs. $1,102.15 Nov 20 close / $1,094.01 Nov 23 snapshot)
web_blocks.how_calculated: We blend 2-year forward EPS ($25.40 FY28E EPS at 10.6% CAGR) with a 39.0x exit P/E, still ~9% above the 35.86x 10-year mean. We cross-check that against an 8.5% WACC DCF ($851–$950 range).
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY26 EPS $20.76; FY26 audited CFO $15,817M and FCF $9,382M; 443.27M shares; 10-year avg P/E 35.86x; consensus 5Y EPS growth 9.81%.
web_blocks.if_off: If Costco sustains >13% EPS growth from faster global openings and retail media profit while rates fall, a 45x–46x multiple could hold.

web_blocks.takeaway: Live snapshot feeds confirm COST trades at $1,094.01 ($484.79B market cap, 52.7x TTM P/E, 43.50x Fwd P/E, 51.64x P/FCF, 28.4% ROE, 21.23% ROIC) in Stage 2 [26, 27].

web_blocks.caption: Costco vs. Listed Retail & Warehouse Club Peers (Nov 20, 2026 Session Benchmark)
web_blocks.takeaway: Costco posts the group's top ROIC at 21.23%, yet its 53.09x P/E and 4.43x–4.47x PEG look steep [26, 27]. It trades far above BJ's (20.3x P/E), Target (15.4x), Amazon (19.9x), and Walmart (49.0x) [26, 27].

web_blocks.mechanism: By late 1999, Walmart was the world's top physical retailer, growing stores and profits steadily. Yet the market priced its shares at ~45x–50x earnings.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: From FY2000 to FY2010, Walmart grew sales from $165B to $408B (+9.5% CAGR) and EPS from $1.25 to $3.72 (+11.5% CAGR). Still, the stock went sideways for over 11 years as its P/E fell from ~48x to ~14x.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Great business growth cannot save buyers from flat multi-year returns when entry multiples top 45x–50x on single-digit sales growth.

web_blocks.title: 7.4 Reverse DCF Sensitivity Matrix & Why 1.92% FCF Yield Leaves Zero Margin of Safety

web_blocks.html: Single-point DCFs can hide fragile inputs, so we stress-test $1,102.15 across a full sensitivity grid [26, 27, 30]. We vary WACC from 8.0% to 9.0% and terminal growth from 3.0% to 4.0% [26, 27, 30]. The math stays unforgiving across every realistic cell. Even with a low 8.0% cost of equity and an aggressive 4.0% terminal growth rate, $488.40 billion still demands ~12.2% annual FCF growth for a decade [16, 27]. That sits well above the 9.81% consensus 5-year EPS growth rate and rising ~$7.5 billion FY2027 capex [16, 27]. At a standard 8.5% WACC and 3.5% terminal growth, a realistic 9.5% FCF CAGR yields $875–$915 per share [30].

Cash yield tells the exact same story. At $1,102.15, Costco's 1.92% trailing FCF yield (52.06x P/FCF; 51.64x on Finviz Nov 23) trails risk-free 5.04% 10-year U.S. Treasuries by 312 basis points [26, 27]. That negative spread leaves buyers reliant on long-term growth and high exit multiples. Suppose trailing P/E drops 20% from 53.09x to 42.5x over two years—still 19% above its 35.86x 10-year mean [27, 28]. Even then, shareholders lose nearly two full years of 10%+ earnings growth just to break even [27, 28]. Meanwhile, Wall Street's $1,101.97 consensus Finviz target price confirms zero upside from $1,102.15 [27].

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Sensitivity: Implied 10-Year FCF CAGR Required to Justify $1,102.15 (Base FCF: $9,382M)
web_blocks.takeaway: Even at 8.0% WACC and 4.0% terminal growth, $1,102.15 bakes in ~12.2%–14.2% 10-year FCF growth. At a realistic 9.5% FCF pace, fair value sits near $850–$950 [30].

web_blocks.html: Valuation Re-Underwriting Trigger: A price reset to $850–$900 (~33x–35x forward EPS) or sustained >13% EPS growth from global openings and retail media would change our valuation verdict.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have completed our price-blind audit and locked in our verdict that Costco is an unmistakable COMPOUNDER_PASS business, we are finally allowed to lift the curtain on the stock ticker. What we see on the screen as of the November 20, 2026 close is a collision between one of the finest retail machines ever built and one of the most demanding price tags in public equity markets: $1,102.15 per share, representing a $488.40 billion market capitalization (and $1,094.01 on the November 23 TradingView snapshot, with Finviz consensus target price sitting at $1,101.97).

Let us put that $488.40 billion valuation into plain English. In FY2026, Costco generated $15,817 million of operating cash flow and $9,382 million of free cash flow after $6,435 million in capital spending. Dividing $9.38 billion by $488.40 billion gives you a trailing free cash flow yield of 1.92%—52.06x P/FCF at the November 20 close and 51.64x on Finviz's November 23 feed. That means if you bought the entire company at today's market price and pocketed every dollar of cash left over after building new warehouses, your starting cash yield would be less than two cents on the dollar—well below risk-free U.S. Treasury yields. On earnings, you are paying 53.09 times trailing net income and 43.50 times forward earnings.

Why is the market willing to pay 53 times earnings for a business that caps its branded markups at 14% and earns a 3.85% operating margin? Because institutional capital prizes certainty above almost everything else. When investors look at Costco, they see $5,907 million in membership fees that recur at a 92.3% U.S. and Canada renewal rate, a negative working-capital cycle that funds expansion out of supplier payables, and a management team that just declared a $30.00 per share special cash dividend—roughly $13.3 billion handed back to owners. Yet remember what that $13.3 billion payout does to the balance sheet: paying $13.3 billion out of $21,301 million cash against $6,162 million of total debt ($2,248 million current maturities) trims net cash from ~$15.1 billion down to ~$1.8 billion ex-leases, cutting FY2027 interest income after $711 million of interest and other income helped FY2026 pre-tax profit.

To test whether $1,102.15 makes sense for your marginal dollar, you and I should run a Reverse DCF—not to predict the future, but to see what the market is already assuming. At an 8.5% discount rate and a 3.5% terminal growth rate, $488.40 billion requires Costco to grow free cash flow at roughly 14.0% to 14.5% every single year for the next decade from our $9,382 million FY2026 base. Think about how hard that is on a $303 billion revenue base. Over the past ten years—including the once-in-a-generation pandemic surge—Costco grew revenue at 9.96% annually, and consensus expects roughly 9.81% EPS growth over the next five years. Meanwhile, management just guided FY2027 capital expenditures up 16.5% to ~$7.5 billion, accrued member rewards rose 13.4% to $3,037 million, and ~$500 million of IEEPA tariffs remain tied up in refunds and three consumer class actions.

History offers a sobering mirror here. At the peak of 1999, Walmart was the undisputed king of global retail. Over the next eleven years, Walmart more than doubled its sales from $165 billion to $408 billion and tripled its earnings per share. Yet shareholders who bought at 48 times earnings in 1999 endured a 'lost decade' of flat stock performance because the multiple compressed back toward earth. That is the exact valuation tension we face with Costco at $1,102.15: the business can execute brilliantly and the stock can still deliver mediocre returns if the P/E normalizes from 53x toward 36x–39x.

Let us push that Reverse DCF one step deeper together, because single-point valuation models can lull you into false precision. When you and I test a stock priced at $1,102.15, we want to see a full sensitivity grid: what happens if the discount rate moves between 8.0% and 9.0%, and what happens if perpetual terminal growth sits between 3.0% and 4.0%? Even if we hand Costco the most generous assumptions on the sheet—an 8.0% cost of equity and a 4.0% perpetual growth rate forever—$488.40 billion still demands roughly 12.2% annual free cash flow growth for ten straight years. At our baseline 8.5% WACC and 3.5% terminal growth, it demands 14.2% FCF growth every year through FY2036.

Now ask yourself whether 14.2% annual FCF compounding on a $303 billion revenue base is a conservative base case. When capex grows faster than revenue to fund 33 gross warehouse openings in FY2027, free cash flow growth naturally lags operating income growth. If Costco compounds free cash flow at a very respectable 9.5% per year—right in line with its 9.96% ten-year revenue CAGR and 9.81% consensus five-year EPS growth—our 8.5% WACC model puts intrinsic value around $875 to $915 per share, right alongside independent DCF benchmarks near $851.

That brings us back to the simplest sanity check in finance: the 1.92% trailing free cash flow yield. When risk-free U.S. Treasuries pay more than 4%, accepting a 1.92% starting cash yield on an equity means you have zero margin of safety against multiple compression. Think about the arithmetic: if Costco's earnings grow 10.6% a year for two years—from $20.76 to $25.40—but its P/E eases just one-fifth of the way down from 53.09x to 42.5x, the stock goes nowhere. And if it normalizes to 39.0x—still higher than its 35.86x ten-year average—you get our $990.00 base-case value, a 10.2% capital loss from $1,102.15.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: GREAT COMPANY VS. GREAT STOCK
book_callouts.text: The hardest discipline in institutional investing is separating admiration for a business from the price of its shares. Costco earns 21.23% ROIC and treats its members with unmatched fairness—but at 53.09x trailing earnings and a 4.43x–4.47x PEG ratio, the market has already collected several years of future compounding upfront.

book_subsections.title: Peer Multiples: Paying Twice BJ's Multiple for Half the Risk?
paragraphs: When you line Costco up against its direct listed peers on the November 20, 2026 tape, the valuation gap jumps off the page. BJ's Wholesale Club—a smaller regional U.S. warehouse club operator—trades at 20.3x trailing earnings ($104.82, $13.24B market cap, 28.9% ROE). Target trades at 15.4x trailing earnings, and Amazon trades at 19.9x trailing earnings. Even Walmart, which has enjoyed its own massive re-rating on grocery share gains and high-margin advertising, sits at 49.0x trailing P/E—still cheaper than Costco despite lower ROIC.

Costco undeniably deserves a structural premium over BJ's and Target because its 21.23% ROIC, 94.9% owned-building footprint, and global scale in 14 countries are in a different league. The analytical question is not whether Costco deserves a premium; it is whether a 34% to 55% premium over Costco's own 10-year historical averages leaves enough upside to clear our 15% annualized return hurdle. Our Reverse DCF and 39x normalized FY2028E multiple point to $990.00 per share as fair value—below both $1,102.15 and Finviz's $1,101.97 target.

book_subsections.title: Duration Risk: Why 53x Earnings Behaves Like a Long-Duration Bond
paragraphs: When you and I evaluate a 53.09x trailing P/E and a 1.92% free cash flow yield, it helps to borrow a concept from fixed income: duration. A stock trading at 15x earnings returns your purchase price in roughly fifteen years of flat earnings; a stock trading at 52x free cash flow pushes the majority of your economic payback decades into the future. That means your near-term return is extraordinarily sensitive to the exit multiple Mr. Market is willing to pay two or three years from now.

Think about how little has to go wrong for a 53x multiple to compress. Costco does not need to suffer a recession or lose its moat. All it takes is for Treasury yields to stay firm, or for comparable-store sales to cool from 6% to 4% while FY2027 capex steps up to $7.5 billion and interest income drops after the $13.3 billion special dividend. If the market decides that a mature $303 billion retailer growing earnings at ~10% deserves 39x forward earnings—still a 9% premium above Costco's own 10-year historical average of 35.86x—then $25.40 of FY2028E EPS values the business at $990.00.
